Below is a draft essay. Revise it so that it reads as if a US grade 8 student wrote it in class for a timed writing test. Keep the position it argues and keep it at about 257 words. The file must contain only the revised essay.

A measurement tool scored the draft on how it carries feeling. For each measure below it gives the current value and a target. Revise the essay so that its measures move to the targets; the tool will score the result again.
- positive charge (hedons per 1,000 words): now 103.6, target 102.5. Counts positive words such as good, love, fun.
- negative charge (dolors per 1,000 words): now 9.7, target 6.9. Counts negative words such as bad, hate, problem.
- words that carry charge (% of words): now 31.3, target 27.7. Counts share of all words that carry any feeling.
- charge under a negation (% of charge): now 3.2, target 2.3. Counts feeling words placed under not, never or n't.
- charge after an intensifier such as 'very' (% of charge): now 0.0, target 0.9. Counts feeling words placed right after very, really or so.
- charge after a contrast word such as 'but' (% of charge): now 0.0, target 7.6. Counts feeling words placed after but or however in the same sentence.
- net charge of the last fifth minus the text's mean (per 1,000 words): now 52.0, target 30.5. Counts how much more positive the last fifth is than the essay as a whole; negative means a more downbeat ending.
- how unevenly charge is spread over sentences (1 = as if words were dealt at random): now 1.1, target 1.4. Counts above 1 means the feeling is bunched into some sentences while others are plain; below 1 means it is spread evenly.

Draft:

Dear Principal,

I am writing about your decision on whether to require community service. I believe every student should be required to do it, as long as the school keeps the hours reasonable and lets students choose how they help.

First, community service teaches things a classroom cannot. My friend Maya tutors second graders at Lincoln Elementary twice a week. She told me that explaining fractions to a seven-year-old made her understand them better herself. She also learned patience and how to talk to people who are frustrated. Those are skills every job will ask for later.

Second, service connects students to the place they live. Last spring a group of us cleaned up litter along the creek behind the park. We filled twenty bags in one afternoon. Now when I walk past that creek, I notice when trash shows up, and I pick it up. I would never have cared about that spot if I had not worked on it.

I understand that some students feel they are already too busy with homework, sports, and jobs. That concern is fair. However, a requirement of around twenty hours a year is less than half an hour a week. The school could also count activities students already do, like coaching a youth team or helping at a church food drive, so it does not feel like an extra burden.

Requiring service would help our community and make us better people. Please consider making it part of what it means to graduate from our school.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Student
